entries.subject: SDSS DR9 color HiPS
entries.finding: SDSS9 color: SDSS g, r and i; 2000 × 2000 px over 7.20 × 7.20 arcmin. The cutout's registration is its request: a tangent projection centred on the nebula's central star, north up.

entries.subject: The shape of the Owl Nebula
entries.finding: García-Díaz et al. (2018, Sect. 3) find that a shell does not fit the spectra: the nebula is a slightly prolate spheroid filled with emission, inclined about 25 degrees with its north-west half toward Earth, with a multipolar cavity carved out of it that emits 0.3 of the gas around it; their velocity channels (Sect. 2.3) need three cavity lobes, one to the north-west toward us and two to the south-east, the more easterly toward us and the more southerly away. Guerrero et al. (2003) give the sizes: an ellipsoid of radius 93 arcsec along the pole and 83 arcsec across it, inside a filled envelope 218 arcsec across, with eyes about 35 arcsec in size and denser gas along the equatorial plane. The bank fills that body with the picture's light. How much the gas emits at each distance from the star, and how long each cavity is along its sight line, are read from the picture.

entries.subject: NOIRLab noao-m97
entries.finding: A 500 x 455 px photograph whose file carries no sky tags, so it cannot be placed without a fit.
entries.revisitWhen: A photograph of the Owl Nebula with sky coordinates is published under an attribution licence.

entries.subject: Stars in the picture
entries.finding: The photograph first kept its stars, which stood on the nebula's plane whatever their own distances. The Nebula Lab's NOX removes them and keeps the nebula's structure. One pass left the saturated stars, tens of pixels wide; a second pass over a quarter-size copy takes them, and the picture takes that pass's result only where it took a star.
